title: Psalm 103: Bless the LORD, O My Soul
summary: The psalmist calls his own soul to bless the LORD and not forget his benefits: forgiveness, healing, redemption, love, and renewal. He then widens the praise to God's dealings with Israel, recalling God's self-description to Moses as compassionate and gracious, a Father who removes sins as far as east from west and remembers that his people are dust. Finally he summons angels, heavenly hosts, and all creation to bless the LORD, and ends where he began, with his own soul.
story: Psalm 103 follows the lament of Psalm 102, and the contrast is deliberate. Both psalms know that human life is as brief as grass (102:11; 103:15), but where Psalm 102 cried out from that frailty, Psalm 103 rests in the everlasting love that surrounds it. Psalms 103 and 104 are twins, both opening and closing with “Bless the LORD, O my soul”: Psalm 103 praises God for his mercy to his people, Psalm 104 for his care of the whole creation. Book IV began with Moses' prayer in Psalm 90, and here Moses returns, as the one to whom God made known his ways.
historical:
The heading is simply “Of David”. As with other headings, scholars differ on whether it records authorship or marks the psalm as part of a Davidic collection. Some features of the Hebrew, including a few late grammatical forms, have led many scholars to date the psalm after the exile; others think those features do not settle the question and accept an earlier date. The psalm itself names no event.

Its theological center is a quotation of Israel's foundational text about God's character. After Israel worshiped the golden calf at Sinai and Moses interceded for them, the LORD passed before Moses and proclaimed himself compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness, forgiving iniquity (Exodus 34:6-7). Verse 8 of this psalm repeats that confession almost word for word, and verse 7 points to the same scene: “He made known His ways to Moses”. That confession is echoed across the Old Testament (Numbers 14:18; Nehemiah 9:17; Joel 2:13; Jonah 4:2), and this psalm is one of its fullest meditations.
cultural:
To bless someone in Hebrew usage was to speak well of them and to acknowledge their goodness, and when people bless God it means to praise him gratefully. The psalm opens with a person addressing his own soul, nephesh, which in Hebrew means the whole living self rather than an immaterial part. The phrase “all that is within me” (verse 1) reinforces that: every part of the person joins in.

Several images come from ordinary life. The eagle (or vulture; the Hebrew word covers large birds of prey) was a picture of vigor, and commentators often suggest the image draws on the way such birds seem renewed after molting their feathers. The compassion of a father for his children (verse 13) drew on the household, where a father was the protector and provider; the psalm says God's compassion is like that. Grass and wildflowers in Israel sprang up after the winter rains and withered within days when the hot east wind blew off the desert, a wind every Israelite knew (verse 16).
literary: The psalm is framed by the same line, “Bless the LORD, O my soul”, at its opening (verses 1 and 2) and its close (verse 22). Between them it widens in circles: from the individual (verses 1 to 5), to Israel and Moses (verses 6 to 18), to the heavenly throne and all creation (verses 19 to 22). The first section lists God's benefits with a string of participles, he who forgives, heals, redeems, crowns, and satisfies. The middle section is built on comparisons: as high as the heavens, as far as east from west, as a father has compassion. It then contrasts human frailty, like grass and flowers, with God's love “from everlasting to everlasting”. The closing summons repeats “Bless the LORD” four times.

outline.t: My soul, do not forget his benefits
Compassionate and gracious: sins removed, frailty remembered
Our days are grass; his love is everlasting
Angels, hosts, and all his works, bless the LORD

doctrines.note: Forgiveness is God's first benefit in the list and the theme of the middle section. He has “not dealt with us according to our sins”, and he removes transgressions as far as east is from west, a distance that can never be closed.
Verse 8 restates God's own description of himself at Sinai: compassionate, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. The psalm presents this as who God is, not a mood he is sometimes in.
“He knows our frame; He is mindful that we are dust.” Human beings are frail and brief, and God's compassion takes that frailty into account rather than holding it against us.
God's everlasting love extends to those who fear him, keep his covenant, and remember his precepts, and to their children's children. Mercy flows within a relationship with obligations on both sides.

words.note: Barak, to bless. When God blesses people he gives them life and good; when people bless God they praise him and acknowledge him as the source of that good. The psalm uses the word six times, making blessing God its main action.

Salach, to forgive. In the Old Testament this verb always has God as its subject; people pardon one another with other words, but salach is God's own act. It opens the list of his benefits in verse 3.

Yetser, frame or form, from the verb used for a potter shaping clay (Genesis 2:7 uses the verb for God forming man from dust). God knows our frame because he made it, and he remembers what it is made of.

Rachum, compassionate. Related to the word for womb, it suggests tender, visceral care. Paired with channun (gracious), it comes from God's self-description in Exodus 34:6 and is almost always used of God.

christ: The psalm's list of benefits, forgiving iniquities and healing diseases, is exactly what Jesus does in the Gospels, sometimes in the same moment, as when he forgives and heals the paralyzed man and his critics ask who can forgive sins but God alone (Mark 2:1-12). Mary's song echoes verse 17 when she says God's mercy is for those who fear him from generation to generation (Luke 1:50). And the New Testament locates the removal of sins as far as east from west in Christ's death, through which God does not count people's trespasses against them (2 Corinthians 5:19). The psalm does not predict these things; it describes the character of God that Christians believe was shown most fully in Jesus.

hard.q: The psalm says God heals all your diseases. What about faithful people who are not healed?
hard.a: Verse 3 sets forgiveness and healing side by side as God's benefits, and many believers have prayed for healing that did not come. The psalm itself answers part of this: verses 15 and 16 say plainly that human life withers like grass and vanishes. It is not promising that no believer will ever be ill or die. Some interpreters read verse 3 as the psalmist's testimony about a particular recovery, generalized into praise; others see all healing, whether through recovery, medicine, or ordinary health, as God's gift; and Christians have also read it in light of the resurrection, when every disease will finally be healed. What the psalm does not allow is the conclusion that illness means God has stopped loving the sick person. Its love is “from everlasting to everlasting”, which outlasts every sickness.

questions: The psalmist has to tell his own soul not to forget. What kinds of God's benefits are you most likely to forget, and why?
What does it mean to you that God “is mindful that we are dust”? Is that comforting, humbling, or both?
The psalm moves from one person's praise to the praise of angels and all creation. How does private gratitude connect to something larger than yourself?
